items.title: More AI Editing Assistance is on the Way as Eddie AI V4 is Unveiled Ahead of IBC 2026
items.summary: IBC 2026 is already off to a hot start before the hall doors at the RAI Amsterdam open in the Netherlands later this week. We’ve gotten big announcements from a ton of major brands so far, and it looks like it will be a packed house with companies big and small, plus thousands of filmmakers and videographers, in attendance. If you’re interested in video editing, and specifically AI-assisted video editing, it looks like we’ll be getting another major update from the team at Eddie AI, as the company has announced that its V4 version will be ready to check out for those there in person. Here’s the latest. Eddie AI V4 Update Promising to be yet another update for the AI assistant editor that seems to get a boost every few months at this point, Eddie AI is getting some more new features and power-ups to make it more than just a single-use AI assistant. And, in truth, this does appear to be the way of the future, as Blackmagic Design has just announced that DaVinci Resolve is getting new AI assistant integration, and Adobe has announced that its AI assistants are now set to be available in After Effects public beta. The latest from Eddie AI follows suit as the company has announced that the tool is moving far beyond simply trimming a timeline; it’s now watching rushes, finding the story, syncing cameras, naming who is on which angle, writing the music, sourcing the b-roll, and handing the finished cut to Premiere, Resolve, Avid, or Final Cut as a real project file. More Updates on the Way? It’s hard to say if and when any of these players in this space, like Eddie AI, might slow down as the industry heats up and gains speed. If this is a space you’re at all interested in, it might be in your best interest to check it out sooner rather than later if you want to keep up. items.title: Adobe Unveils New Generative Media Tool in Premiere, Plus More AI-Powered Updates
items.summary: Believe it or not, more AI-powered tools and upgrades are coming to Premiere and After Effects. In fact, Adobe is also rolling out a new Generative Media Tool directly in Premiere that lets users generate video and sound effects in their timelines. And while the direction of these new updates and features is not surprising, as Adobe has been developing AI tools and features for several years now, the addition of more of them directly in Premiere (and After Effects) is a bit new, as until now most of the major new AI innovations have been in the Firefly video editor. Still, this is big news coming out of IBC 2026, where the company is showcasing these updates on the floor. Let’s take a look at everything new here in Premiere and After Effects and explore what might be the most useful for your workflows. Adobe Premiere’s Generative Media Tool As Adobe has shared before, the company’s latest Creators' Toolkit Report found that nearly 90% of its creators “accelerate the growth of their business or audience” when they use AI tools like the ones in Adobe’s suite. And that continues to be the direction of the company, and most companies these days, as Adobe has unveiled Premiere’s new Generative Media tool, which will now allow editors to generate video and sound effects directly in their Premiere timelines. The new tool promises to be quite intuitive and easy to use, as all you’ll need to do is simply select the tool and define what you want to appear. You just describe what you need, and Premiere will generate context-aware, fully editable video and audio clips that you can refine and iterate on without leaving the project. At launch, users will be able to choose from different models, including Adobe Firefly and partner models like Google Veo, Kling, Runway, and Luma. Some of the other new tools in the taskbar will also include: Generate Video: Editors can generate video to fill gaps in their timeline, using reference frames sampled from their project to create footage

items.title: 'Godzilla Minus Zero' Full Trailer Breakdown: "This Isn't Godzilla We Are Talking About"
items.summary: That shake of your home or apartment is not an earthquake; it's the coming of a monster with such scope and scale that it rattles the earth. In the initial 30-second teaser for Godzilla Minus Zero, we got a brief taste of the post-war dread returning to Japan. Now, with the full trailer, we can see what's in store for the IMAX experience. Director Takashi Yamazaki isn't holding back, and neither are any of the incredible VFX artists who worked on the movie. This new trailer gives us our clearest look yet at the stakes, the cast, and a twist that changes everything we thought we knew about the sequel. Check out the full trailer below. - YouTube www.youtube.com "We Didn't Finish the Job" The trailer opens with ominous dialogue confirming our fears from the first movie: the initial onslaught by Godzilla was not stopped; he survived and now wants revenge. Human victory was temporary, and the battle will wage on. Operation Narukami & Plan B So, how do you take out a creature like Godzilla? Well, you need a plan. In the trailer, we see a war room filled with military officials and scientists debating how to handle the creature's return. The consensus? "Fight fire with fire." Sure, that seems like a good idea! It's also the plant for what kind of fire they could possibly dig up that would match Godzilla...perhaps another creature? Ms. Aoyama proposes "Plan B," which I think is tied to Operation Narukami. It has the blessing of the military, and we see people mobilizing to take it on. The Twist So, at the very end of the trailer, we see Godzilla's body fall from the sky and hear a distinct kind of pterodactyl cry. A lot of theories think this is King Ghidorah, who maybe the officials released to fight Godzilla, or who maybe is already terrorizing the nation, recontextualizing everything you've seen so far. items.title: If Writing Feels Easy, You're Doing It Wrong
items.summary: R.F. Kuang is 29 and has already published seven novels, including the Nebula-winning Babel, the #1 New York Times bestseller Yellowface, and this year's Katabasis. She trained at Cambridge, Oxford, and Yale. In a recent "How I Write" interview with David Perell, she walked through how she approaches writing scenes, from the physical construction of emotion to why the hardest writing sessions produce her best work. Granted, Kuang works in prose, not screenplays. But most of what she says translates easily to other areas of writing. Here are four ideas from the conversation any screenwriter can steal. - YouTube www.youtube.com Emotion Is Physiological If you've ever been in therapy, your therapist might have asked you to be more specific about the emotions you were feeling—for instance, where in the body do they sit? What are the sensations you're getting as a result of emotions? Kuang does the same with students, which helps them avoid reaching for the same tired emotion words we all might use. "I passed out these kindergarten-level silhouette diagrams of the human body, and I [said], without reaching for any abstractions, tell me how joyous triumph—suppose you just got a call and you got a promotion. Tell me where that sits in the body. Describe only what is happening on a physical level." Students reported elevated heart rates, palpitations, butterflies. One student said her toes tingled with joy. In a novel, a writer would be able to express everything a character is feeling internally, but in a screenplay, you have to think about this on a visual level. Does stress make a character sweat? Does great emotion fill their eyes with tears? Does fear make their gaze dart around? Even when you're limited to what we can see, you can be super creative. This is the show, don't tell advice you've probably heard before. Instead of writing "She felt scared," write what the body is doing. items.title: Nikon Announces New Firmware Update for the Nikon ZR, Plus a Roadmap for Future Upgrades
items.summary: A new firmware update is here for the Nikon ZR, which is good news. There’s also more good news: the company has shared plans for major new features like open gate recording and a desqueeze display, but those updates aren’t set to be incorporated into the ZR until 2027. So, a bit of good news and a potential future good news situation here. Still, Nikon’s announcement of its upcoming firmware version 2.00 for the ZR isn’t nothing, and it does show a good sign of things to come. Although if any owners or potential owners were expecting more, it’s understandable to wish that all the good news were here already. Let’s look at what’s on the roadmap as of right now. Nikon ZR Firmware Update Announcement Today’s announcement from Nikon is that firmware version 2.00 for the Nikon ZR, released about a year ago today as the company’s first full-frame sensor camera in the Z Cinema series and as part of the new era following Nikon’s acquisition of RED Digital Cinema, is coming soon. Here’s a full list of the features planned for inclusion in this firmware update, aimed at further advancing reactive capabilities and workflows for a wide range of ZR users, including high-end filmmakers and run-and-gun content creators. Support for Log3G10 and REDWideGamutRGB when recording in H.265 format, delivering compact file sizes with high color-grading latitude. A new option for selecting the level of [High ISO NR] available during H.265 Log recording, enabling image rendering tailored to the creator’s intent and the tone of the work. Support for focus peaking display during recording in the R3D NE* format, enabling more precise focus confirmation. This firmware version 2.00 is scheduled to release later this year, although a date has not yet been revealed. items.title: Western Movie Villains Who Stole the Show
items.summary: Is there anything better than a Western villain? In the lawless frontier, they are usually a man who takes what he wants, regardless of who it hurts, and wields power ruthlessly. The genre's villains sometimes work harder than the heroes to provide an easy-to-understand threat that scares the audience. These five performances did that and more, changing the genre for the better. Some are the film's actual antagonists, some are memorable faces in a bigger evil, and a couple were played by actors so associated with heroism that their turn to menace was shocking. Regardless, every time they're on screen, they steal the show. What does it take to steal a Western from the lead? Let's look at these roles to find out. - YouTube www.youtube.com Henry Fonda in Once Upon a Time in the West This was Sergio Leone's most audacious bit of casting. America's on-screen father figure, who had played Tom Joad, Wyatt Earp, Mister Roberts, and the president, was introduced here by executing a child on his family's porch. Henry Fonda shocked as Frank. The Spaghetti Western focuses on a fight over valuable land and its water source. Leone reportedly rejected Fonda's brown contacts and beard, wanting the blue eyes and a clean-shaven look so the audience would know it was him. "When he sent me the script, I couldn't believe it," Fonda told Dick Cavett, "and I didn't accept it, but he flew to California and persuaded me." Casting against type is a way to weaponize an audience's memory of every hero the actor has ever played. Fonda's face carried 30 years of American virtue, so to turn that into fear was no easy feat. Leone made him into the film's opening threat. - YouTube www.youtube.com Jane Darwell in The Ox-Bow Incident Henry Fonda shows up in this one, too, but he's not the villain. items.title: Inside Hollywood’s Biggest Summer Box Office Ever
items.summary: Are you ready for some great news out of Hollywood? We just witnessed an all-time record of $4.76 billion (unadjusted for inflation) at the summer box office. This feels like the first great headline since before COVID, and I want to take a minute to celebrate everyone who released movies and wrote scripts, the crews, the execs, and anyone who struck out and chased their dreams. This was the summer for you. Back to the headline, the summer of 2026 beat the previous high watermark of $4.75 billion set in 2013, which stood for 13 years. This new number shattered all predictions and showed that people want to go to the movies, as long as the movies are good. One of the coolest things about this summer, aside from the A/C in the theaters, was that all four months (May through August) cleared $1 billion apiece. That has never ever happened before. Want to learn how we got the biggest box office summer of all time? Let's dive in. Two Titans Carried the Weight Much like the Barbenheimer Summer, we had two movies that bore most of the weight in making this the best ever. First up, Spider-Man: Brand New Day redefined what we know as a Marvel blockbuster and raised the bar even higher. While it's still in theaters and its box office is rising, we can talk about the numbers as they stand now. As of today, we're seeing it at $923 million domestic. If it keeps earning, it has a real shot to beat the Star Wars: The Force Awakens’ all-time domestic record ($936.6M). Then you have Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, which stands at $589 million and change domestic. Together, these films dominated the cultural conversation and helped drive people to theaters en masse. Universal and Sony Take the Crown Studios were important to the success of the summer. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: William Shatner's Captain Kirk Monologue That Defines What 'Star Trek' is All About
items.summary: Star Trek is one of the most hopeful shows on Television. It has inspired generations (pun intended) by encouraging people to explore, be the best version of themselves, and take risks. But underneath all the futuristic tech, aliens, and diplomatic missions, Star Trek is ultimately about the human spirit and what it takes to survive in this galaxy. It can be hard to really put into words what makes the franchise tick. I mean, this thing has spawned movies, series,s and has been around for sixty years. But if you want a quote that gets Star Trek perfectly right, you have to go back to the original show, to a speech from William Shatner's Captain Kirk that lays out the entire ethos of Starfleet in a single speech. Let's dive in. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question Okay, you know the deal with Star Trek: it's about a spaceship flying around for Starfleet, righting wrongs and learning things in outer space. Well, in Season 2, Episode 18, titled "Return to Tomorrow," the crew of the Enterprise encounters three disembodied, highly advanced alien minds housed in glowing spheres. This is one of the most famous episodes of all time and was totally mind-blowing in the 60s when it aired, and even now. items.title: The First-Ever Fisheye Zoom Lens for Sony E-Mount System Cameras is Here
items.summary: For a company with a legacy as deep as Sony, getting a “first-ever” in pretty much any category is kind of a big deal. So it’s cool to see a new lens for Sony E-mount system shooters that has never existed before, as this new FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G Lens is set to be the first-ever fisheye zoom option. Set to feature a full 180-degree angle of view across its 8 to 14mm zoom range, and bringing a nice mix of optical quality and versatility with its constant f/3.5 maximum aperture and 5.9” minimum focus distance, this new fisheye zoom could be a nice option for a wide variety of photo, video, and hybrid shooters. Let’s check it out. Sony FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G Lens As mentioned above, it’s not too often a “first-ever” lens is added to a system as deep and robust as the Sony E-mount system. Still, a gap remained, and this new Sony FE 8-14mm f/3.5 Fisheye G Lens fills it with its full 180-degree angle of view across its zoom range. This fisheye option aims to deliver its own unique perspective across whatever shots you may be looking to capture with stills, video, or even VR imaging. When used with a full-frame Sony E-mount camera, the lens can switch from a circular fisheye at 8mm to a diagonal fisheye at 14mm, which should help maintain ideal composition in each frame, whether for photography or videography. The lens will feature two linear motors for fast, precise autofocus with minimal focus breathing, plus dedicated focus, zoom, and aperture rings to support control. items.title: Paul Greengrass' 5 Best Movies, Ranked
items.summary: British filmmaker Paul Greengrass is known for his tight, frenetically edited action thrillers with an emphasis on true stories, as well as three of the five entries in the Jason Bourne franchise. Let’s look at the five movies of his that are most worth your time from bottom to top. The Lost Bus The Lost Bus premiered at the Toronto International Film Festival in 2025, and follows Matthew McConaughey and America Ferrera as real-life heroes who successfully transported a school bus full of children through a raging wildfire in Northern California in 2018. Greengrass is most commonly heralded for his handling of tight, chaotic thriller sequences with close, shallow camera work, shaky movements, and frenetic editing. And while The Lost Bus still has plenty of these moments everywhere you look, the film also boasts some quite stunning blocked, drone-oriented camera work through wooded areas that often blend practical and special effects with wonderful fluidity. Like all of his true tragedy/disaster oriented films, while the action and intensity is center stage, there is a clear message and heart at the center of the film that often sneaks up quietly during moments you may not anticipate. For a film that, to many, started rockily with questionable character exploration, the film concludes with a total gut punch. The Bourne Supremacy ‘The Bourne Supremacy’Credit: Universal Pictures The second chapter in the original Bourne trilogy is probably the least talked about of the original three, but it still boasts some wonderful kinetic action, and progresses Bourne’s character in increasingly compelling ways. Where many future action films after the Bourne franchise slipped up when attempting to replicate the shaky cam style of shooting that these films partially revolutionized was using it as a crutch to hide stunts.
